speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence by adding my words of congratulation to the Mover and Seconder of the Throne Speech.
It sounds platitudinous to say that the New Democratic Party is dedicated to a new national health plan, but one proof of the sincerity of this dedication is the leadership in both hospital and medicare plans introduced by our colleagues from Saskatchewan. The aspiration to a genuine national health arrangement is not unique to the New Democrats. It is clear, however, that alone among political parties we have the conception of a national health plan, Government-sponsored, comprehensive in both items, coverage and those covered.
The terms "medicare", "national health plan", and "Government-sponsored health plan" have been so bandied about by politicians, a royal commission, insurance companies, the Press and medical associations for so long that the health needs of Canadians have been nearly lost in verbiage. It is much like our search for a national identity. We have been so preoccupied with what we are not that we have lost sight of what we are, or what we should be.
In assigning guilt for our medicare confusion, the Liberal Party, the National Liberal Party, merits the largest measure. It is the most guilty of all because it has promised for the longest, has had the most opportunity to act and has done nothing. Again, in this Throne Speech of 1965, the rosy promise -vague, tantalizing and unsupported-has been resurrected. This strikes us as tawdry politics. Has not the government the advantage of the Hall Commission Report showing the need, the urgency and the right kind of medicare? Of course it has; but even so, the Liberal Party has not assumed the responsibility required by the Hall Report. One can imagine medicare as a nettle that the Liberal Party will parade around with on a platter but refuse, for the poorest of reasons, to grasp in hand and carry.
The Liberals have promised a Government-sponsored health plan since 1919. They have been in power 33 of the past 46 years. I have here a copy of the Toronto Star dated April 21, 1948, from which I should like to quote. This Liberal newspaper is so old that it may fall apart, just like the Liberal promises.
The article states:
Health insurance at once said plan of Premier King.
April 7. 1965

The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe
In the body of the article appears the following statement:
The goal of the national health insurance and the social security scheme is that all Canadians will be covered by it and all Canadians will be contributing toward its cost.
This sounds very modern, much like what we are asking for today, but still we are waiting.
Another pamphlet that I should like to quote from is one that the Liberal Party itself brought out during its campaign in 1963, and which is entitled "The Policies of the Liberal Party". At page 15 appears an article entitled "Caring for Health".
Underneath that heading the following is stated:
Establish, in co-operation with the Provinces, a medical care plan for all Canada.
It also states:
The Liberal plan for student scholarships and loans will enable more people to become doctors.
Then it speaks of more people becoming doctors; but the student loan legislation brought out by the Liberal Government, because of its excessive costs and the longevity of the course-and of course there are still no scholarships-does not encourage students to study medicine.
Another 1963 Liberal publication is entitled "Health Care as Needed", and sets out a promise for prepaid care, which is available to everyone, on terms which everyone can afford. It says that all Canadians should be able to get health care at the time they need it, without the anxious fear of bills they cannot afford. Again, this was very modem in its conception and is related to something that has been going on since 1919. But it is still nothing but a promise.
In June of 1964 the Hall Royal Commission Report on Health Services was tabled in the House of Commons. Even its most urgent recommendations have thus far been ignored. There have been many promises, and more thousands of words, but still no action has been taken. The Minister who should be responsible talks a good game on medicare. We suspect she has thought out the course ahead and has had the tactical ability to foul it up, even more adequately than she did the National Pension Plan. From the original promise of 1919 to the "health care at once" of 1948, to the party platform in 1963 and to the words in the House of Commons in 1964 and 1965, how does one go about orientating oneself in these Liberal semantics?

[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The New Democratic Party has always stood very clearly for an all-inclusive, completely comprehensive, compulsory, Government-sponsored national health plan. The plan includes doctors' care, dental care, drugs, glasses and prosthetic appliances. It postulates increased educational facilities for doctors, nurses and technicians, for preventive medicine and badly needed research facilities. The New Democratic Party stands firmly in support of all these provisions. We stand firmly against high cost partial plans, against deterrent fees and particularly against the indignity of means testing.
I should like to take the Hall Commission Report and quote from the actual charter set out in the Report:
The achievement of the highest possible health standards for all our people must become a primary objective of national policy and a cohesive factor contributing to national unity, involving individual and community responsibilities and actions. This objective can best be achieved through a comprehensive, universal, health services program for the Canadian people implemented in accordance with Canada's evolving constitutional arrangements, based upon freedom of choice and upon free and self-governing professions and institutions, financed through prepayment arrangements, accomplished through the full co-operation of the general public, the health professions, voluntary agencies, all political parties, and governments, federal, provincial and municipal, directed toward the most effective use of the nation's health resources to attain the highest possible levels of physical and mental wellbeing.
Within this report, however, there are certain recommendations considered to be urgent enough that the Commission advised their implementation within six months of the tabling of the Report. They are as follows:
1.	A Federal-Provincial conference. This is what the Government now suggests in the Speech from the Throne 10 months after the report was tabled, in which it was said that this was something urgent that should be done within the first six months. We should be working on the recommendations of such a conference instead of discussing its inclusion in the Throne Speech.
2.	The inclusion of mental and t.b. care under the Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act.
3.	A crash program of health personnel training and education.
4.	A children's dental program.
5.	The provision of services to crippled and mentally retarded children.
6.	Expansion of the Medical Research Council into a Health Sciences Research Council.
April 7, 1965
The urgency of these steps was stressed. It has been underlined again and again by Mr. Justice Hall. Nine and a half months later no action on any of these urgent matters is yet in sight. In its more specific recommendations the Report goes on to stress the following necessities: First, crash programs to provide personnel, hospitals, research into mental illness and retardation, drug addiction and alcoholism; a long list of medical services, including medical, surgical, maternity, preventive, ambulance, etc.; dental personnel, facilities and free care for children and expectant mothers and the fluoridation of municipal water supplies; the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on drugs and the provision of prescription drugs over $1; free optical services for all, including free glasses for children; greater facilities, scholarships and salary funds for all phases of medical education, and vastly increased medical research funds, which recommendation, incidentally, has been echoed strongly by the Medical Research Council.
The Report recommends strongly against partial, non-compulsory plans, against means testing and against deterrent fees. Yet, Mr. Speaker, in the presence of these urgent recommendations this Government is standing by and watching Province after Province come up with schemes which this report has so strongly recommended against. It is hard to blame the Provinces for this variety, this developing crazy quilt. Why? Because the Federal Government continues to abdicate its responsibilities.
To this date, half the Provinces of Canada have established or announced plans for establishing their own medical care schemes. Under the C.C.F., Saskatchewan set up the first and only universal, comprehensive, medical care scheme, now functioning well and covering 99.8 per cent of its population. This scheme would readily fit into a comprehensive Federal plan. Alberta's plan, better known as "minicare", fails to cover the low income groups which need it most. It employs a form of means test and the benefits supplied are minimal. Both Ontario and British Columbia have given up waiting for Federal action and have outlined plans for coverage similar to Alberta's, again with a means test and a subsidy to those unable to pay premiums. Needless to say, the private insurance companies are delighted. They will now have Government subsidized profits. Most recently Quebec has announced its intention to establish its own health scheme. In at least three Provinces, Alberta, Ontario and British
The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe Columbia, the schemes are or will be such as to conflict seriously with a Federal, universal, comprehensive plan. The Government's delaying tactics have only intensified the problem.
What a fantastic anachronism that anyone today should suffer the indignity of a means test. Such a concept extends both indigency and indignity in providing our fellow Canadians with charity. Ask yourself the question: Should there be a means test in education other than the means test of ability? Of course not, and it is even less defensible in health. Our fellow Canadians do not want charity. They simply want the advantages of the best medical treatment.
For now, for the future, is quality medical treatment only for those with the financial means to afford it? This is the present attitude of medical associations in North America. It seems to be, for the want of a clear expression of intent, the present policy of the Government.
What are the barriers which prevent the full institution of the recommended national health services program? I believe there are two. Each is a pressure group, a lobby, an influence against coherent, constructive change.
First there are the private insurance companies. No one in politics nor in the insurance game has ever denied that the two old parties get much of their financial support from them. I should like to quote from statements made by such company spokesmen when the Hall report was tabled. Remember that the predecessors of these men opposed the first old age pension plan, unemployment insurance and government directed hospital insurance. Mr. G. L. Holmes, the manager of the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company, said:
I don't like anything to be given free to people if they can pay for it or part of it. This is what happened to hospital insurance and now people are using hospitals too much. We will all have to pay increased taxes.
J. T. Bryden, Vice President of the North American Life Assurance Company, said:
I do not agree with the philosophy of full medical care for all out of the public purse. Each citizen should shoulder his own responsibilities.
Vice President T. E. Gill of the London Life Insurance Company said that a medicare plan would just be another strain on the economy and that private enterprise can do the job cheaper. Vice President W. J. Adams of the Canada Life Assurance Company said that he doubted that the government could finance medical care cheaper than private companies, and that the universal hospital

April 7, 1965

The Address-Mr. W. D. Howe insurance scheme had cost four or five times more than was originally anticipated. It is obvious where the interests of these people lie.
The second and stronger source of opposition to a genuine national health porgram is the doctors themselves and their associations. Doctors arguing against a medicare plan consistently reveal only selfish motives rather than concern for public needs. A Globe and Mail editorial puts it this way:
Many persons have become suspicious of doctors' opinions in this matter, believing that in some cases their self-interest may outweigh their humanitarian principles.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The most frightening aspect of doctors' intransigence is the blindness of doctors to logical trends within their own profession. And by their blindness they also set themselves apart from and superior to all other professions. For example, is there any greater responsibility for integrity and dedication than that of the teaching profession? Relative to doctors, have teachers failed in a professional sense to adjust their functions and ideals to developing society? I do not think so. Yet teachers have done their work almost universally in Canada under the protective guidance of government administration, both municipal and provincial. There is nothing in this contention of organized medicine, that a Government-sponsored comprehensive plan is innately destructive of their professional ethics. And, of course, Saskatchewan in a short time has proved it is not a blight on their pocketbooks.
Another aspect of doctors' astigmatism is their inability to see how the development of "clinic" medicine and the enlargement of hospital services have been in response to the doctors' own refusal to carry on with the old idea of the all-purpose doctor working alone. In co-operation with the multi-division of responsibility has come advances in research, technique, quality, and much better working conditions for doctors.
The doctors rehash the old argument of quantity rather than quality as a real danger in our projected health program. This is an admission that the needs of the people are greater than we are able to supply at present. How will they meet this ideal? The only answer seems to be by the vagaries of the market's attractiveness to potential doctors and dentists.
Does this mean that only those who can afford it should get the latest and best treatment? Does this mean that we have two classes of citizens, and that second class

citizens do not deserve the best of care? This may have been great, believable stuff in the old days of Queen Victoria when the theory was that the poor are always with us. It is indefensible today.
Rather than restrict the care of these people, would it not be more to the point to provide more facilities for the education of doctors, so that we can provide full care for all who need it? Evidently this Government does not think so. Replying to a question on September 16, 1964, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) indicated that, in view of the fact that any new medical school would take eight years to produce doctors, "this matter will have to wait for an announcement on over-all Government policy". How does one follow such negative reasoning?
Doctors speak of potential excessive demand for services. Would the demand really be excessive? Is this not simply an admission that present care is inadequate?
It is my considered opinion that present methods, costs and facilities, do not allow everyone to get the medical care that is necessary. If they were provided as they should be, one could not consider such usage as "excessive demand".
So, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would like to say that any Government that is genuinely responsible to the people it serves cannot do less than this: to give them the most basic of all services in a way that does not grant charity, that does not destroy human dignity, and provides the best in modern medical care to all who are ill. Surely this is the least that can be done.
This can only be done by a Government-sponsored, universal medical care program, not eight years from now, not four years from now, but immediately. Procrastination, the refusal to care and dare, eternal compromise; these are qualities that have become the fetish of Liberal politicians in the health field. The New Democratic Party insists it is not good enough.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to take part in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I would be remiss if I failed to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cashin) and the seconder (Mr. Chretien). They carried out their task magnificently and did honour to their constituents.
April 7, 1965

[Text}
I also wish to congratulate the hon. Member for Westmorland (Mrs. Rideout) on the marvellous maiden speech she made this afternoon.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, in view of the great number of measures proposed to us in the speech from the throne, we cannot but rejoice and also congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his cabinet for preparing such a wide and far reaching program. We see there an indication that the government does not want to shirk its responsibilities and after two years in office it shows its vigour and determination to tackle all problems. Everyone seems to agree that Parliament has a tremendous amount of work to do and yet all are unanimous in saying that almost all the proposed measures are necessary and urgent.
Once again the present government shows that it is a responsible government and it challenges all hon. members to face up to their responsibilities and, for the general good of the country, to pass without delay this session's program.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) called the speech from the throne an "election manifesto", stating further that it was full of "nebulous promises" taken from previous election platforms and even from other countries. Personally, I do not need to know who are the promoters of some of those measures; I am only interested in seeing them there, included in a program soon to be implemented by an active, even though a minority government, anxious to serve the best interests of the country by carrying out in a responsible way the mandate given to it following the last general election. The press generally had been rather critical of the government in the last few months, accusing it of inaction, backtracking and indecision. But it was comforting last week end to read the comments about the results achieved in the past two years.
It is much to the credit of the Prime Minister, a man who is recognized as an authority on international affairs and who every day shows that he has all the qualities of a great statesman when it comes to solving our domestic problems. Some do not like his method; they would like him to make more noise and indulge in great controversies as some others do. But we, who are close to him, cannot but appreciate the kindness and
The Address-Mr. haniel humanity he brings to the study of great and small problems and rejoice to see the results he achieves.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the very basis of that heavy legislative program is one of the measures included in it, namely the reform of the parliamentary procedure and the adoption of some recommendations made to the house by the committee on procedure and organization. These changes would certainly result into a more expeditive dispatch of the business of the house, and indirectly they would give us the opportunity to show the people that we are able to carry out the business of government as real administrators, without for all that jeopardizing democracy. I hope that this reform will include a suggestion I made in the house on July 15 last to allow the members who wish to do so, to leave their speeches with the Clerk so that they may be taken as read as it is done in Washington.
It is a custom with which the house is not completely unfamiliar since this occurs regularly when the ministers ask for the unanimous consent of the house to table answers which are too long or in the case of long statements.
This way we would avoid a prolonged debate and a continuous repetition of arguments after a number of speeches.
At the time the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said that my proposal was ridiculous under a British-inspired parliamentary system, but I am entirely at variance with him, especially since we already have a few restrictions and limitations. The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne is limited and so is the speaking time allocated to each member. Occasionally, we also limit the duration of certain debates on the consensus of all the various parties. Why should we not be free to change our rules? Why balk at evolution? The Leader of the Opposition is considered as a parliamentarian of great experience but he should not, by refusing his consent to a change in the standing orders, run the risk of finding himself practically isolated here some day.
Many young members have come here full of enthusiasm and you can be certain that the long debates of the last session and the complexity of our parliamentary system are such that some of them wonder how long they will continue to belong to a Government organization which is too often more disappointing than satisfactory.
Mr. Speaker, during the forthcoming months we will continue to hear the voice of
April 7. 1965

The Address-Mr. Laniel those who claim that the present government wants to destroy confederation and divide Canada, but I am satisfied that their number is decreasing constantly. The population realizes increasingly that our government has assumed its responsibilities with regard to the problem of Canadian unity and has already asserted unequivocally its intention to do its utmost to develop a better understanding between the two founding nations. The Laurendeau-Dunton commission has not yet found a magic formula, but its recent report is a warning to those who pursue an ostrichlike policy and attach no great importance to the urgency of finding a solution which would bring all Canadians closer together. Following the recent hearings of the commission in Montreal and Toronto, we have noticed an improvement over last year's situation and the various briefs submitted are an indication that the people as a whole are more conscious of bilingual and bicultural problems and of the importance of a dialogue. Let the Laurendeau-Dunton commission pursue its task, let us stop criticizing it, and let us be confident that 1967 will be noted for this sense of unity and understanding which is everyone's wish.
The dialogue is open at the level of the people; it is making great progress at the level of the federal and provincial governments where the responsibilities are scrutinized and where the fiscal problem is being considered thoroughly.
During that time we are all evolving toward a greater Canadianism which takes into account each one's claims. This is the best safeguard against some dangers referred to by opponents of the formula for repatriation of the constitution. I believe it represents a first step which will serve as a basis for the development of this constitutional agreement between the ten Canadian provinces. I do agree that the British North America Act must be rejuvenated, and this as soon as possible, but between this and saying that a new constitution can be written overnight, there is quite a margin, and I am inclined to believe that words are easier than deeds.
I wish to congratulate Mr. Faribault and Mr. Fowler for their recent essay on the constitution entitled "Ten for One". Their proposals may offer a basis on which other constitutional experts could continue the dialogue and finally put forward ideas which will give our governments the way to find a solution. It should, however, be recognized that Canada presently is changing at a dizzy speed and that some ideas expressed today are often

made obsolete the day after by events and numerous problems that arise. This is why I am rather inclined to believe we are presently writing the new constitution, that we are in the process of writing it every day and that our rapid evolution will lead us to a position where we may more easily agree on most of the provisions which may define the jurisdictions, the responsibilities, each other's rights and the sharing of taxation powers. I agree with the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska when he says, and I quote:
An entirely new draft of the 1867 act appears to me, at the moment, when everything is under discussion, where everything is fluid, not only impossible, but dangerous. Even if co-operative federalism does not reject it for the future.
Theorists in constitutional matters do not agree on the formula for repatriation, but I place my trust in our Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and the experts from the ten provinces who, after lengthy consultations, have agreed upon an amending procedure which will allow us to Canadianize the B.N.A. Act. The dialogue is opened on the evolution of Canada, and it will become livelier as soon as we show our good will by making this first step which is a start toward the adoption of a new constitution or the improvement of the present one.
Those who do not have any responsibility for the affairs of this country may very well advance many theories. The time for intransigence no longer exists; we must trust one another and we must not neglect the advantages of a gradual evolution which will lead us toward better results without upheaval or turmoil.
In his speech, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition tried to ridicule the Government position, he put the emphasis on the differing views of those who do not approve the Fulton-F'avreau formula. And yet, he has not given any indication as to whether he supported all the views of those people, and even less, whether he had the confidence of those people on this problem of national unity. Our Prime Minister has proven more than once his concern for this problem of national unity and he has shown his sincerity in bringing about these measures which, in the long run, will strengthen Canada.
I admit that the adoption of a distinctive national flag will not solve all our problems, no more than the adoption of "O Canada" as our national anthem, but, there, we have the recognition of our sovereignty; those are small things that play on our heart strings
April 7, 1965

and prepare us for a better dialogue. Those symbols are factors of unity which Canadians will increasingly endorse while trying in an exchange of views to understand and appreciate each other better.
On April 1, 1965, in the British House of Commons, Prime Minister Harold Wilson said and I quote:
Nobody here has the monopoly of concern-
Those words apply especially well to the members of this house. Some could surely ponder over this sentence, because the opposition seems to feel sometimes that it is the sole depository of the truth, the only one to see things clearly and to be qualified to pass judgment on Canadian as well as on international problems.
Well, on the Government side, we put action before words. Our achievements up to date show it and the speech from the throne is a still more tangible proof. It covers everything, from international affairs to the war against poverty, from the repatriation of the constitution to a public assistance plan, from the creation of a science council to measures intended to increase sharply the income of our farmers, from assistance to depressed areas to increased assistance to workers displaced by automation; I could go on for quite a while.
All these measures are considered realistically; none will be taken on the sly. Some of them, however, call for negotiations with the provinces and the speech from the throne is a clear indication that it is the intention of the Government to keep on improving the methods and practices governing federal-provincial relations, so that all Canadians can feel they get their fair share out of confederation. This means that we want to intensify our talks with the provinces and seek solutions with them.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, quite disappointing, of course, is that program of action to some of the Members of the Opposition and to their party. The Conservative amendment did not take anyone by surprise. What else could they say? They did not succeed in five years in giving our country any good leadership, and they cannot suffer any action by others which pinpoints more precisely their inaction during those five years.
I was more surprised by the subamendment from the New Democratic Party Leader. He surely has noticed in the Speech from the Throne "the intention of the Government to
The Address-Mr. Laniel meet with the Provinces in order to discuss with them the way in which Federal and Provincial action can most effectively contribute to programs that will provide health services to Canadians on a comprehensive basis". Is this not an indication of positive action to be taken afterwards by the Federal Government in view of giving the lead in that field toward a solution that could be approved by the Provinces? We succeeded in making the Pension Plan a national one because of consultation, and it could not be otherwise for any medicare program.
The speech of the Hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) gave me the definite impression that he does not approve of consultation with the Provinces. This is quite a different attitude from that of the Leader of his party in the Province of Quebec, Mr. Robert Cliche. Mr. Cliche in all his recent speeches takes the attitude that he is promoting a complete dialogue with the Provinces, and he tries very hard to show himself as the great defender of Provincial autonomy. If the National Leader of the New Democratic Party expresses opinions the way he did yesterday toward consultation with the Provinces in regard to the repatriation of the Constitution and concerning the establishment of a national, complete health insurance program, we are inclined to have doubts about his whole attitude toward Federal-Provincial conferences.
Taking these facts into account, I come to the conclusion that his subamendment is not less than a vote of confidence on the whole principle of consultation with the Provinces and also a vote against the positive actions of this Government in that field. Because of the principle involved, Mr. Speaker, this subamendment should be defeated by a roaring majority.

Mr. Speaker, the government is setting steadily to work again and its forward looking policy does not make it forget the present issues. It is endeavouring to co-ordinate all efforts to make Canada a united, strong and prosperous country, where poverty will be enemy number one. It wanted its operations to rest upon a dialogue and we are now faced with a subamendment that condemns, in itself, the principle of true federal provincial relations. We owe it to ourselves to defeat it with an overwhelming majority, in the hope that the members of the party that moved it will realize that they still do not understand the problem of Canadian unity.
April 7, 1965

The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to add my congratulations to the hon. Member tor St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) for their contribution in opening the debate on the Speech from the Throne. I want particularly to pick up a segment of the speech of the hon. Member for St. John's West in a minute and dwell on it for a little while. But first of all I want to make a few general remarks with regard to the Speech from the Throne.
It seems to me that this is a Speech which came out of the Liberal Univac machine or computer. It seems to me that they went around with their mandarins and their eggheads, had some questions asked and put the answers into a computer. There is a little bit of doubt as to where the computer is located; whether it is here in Ottawa or in Washington. It would seem that this Speech from the Throne is, sort of, the left-over breakfast from President Johnson's Great Society Campaign. It is a little bit sad to think that the Liberal Party could not devise some sort of platform for Canada that was not based on Americanism, that was not brought up and hatched in our neighbour to the South.
It seems to me that this Speech from the Throne, as others have said before me, is remarkable for what it has left out; it is remarkable in that it has not done anything or has not suggested anything to cure the rampant Liberal inflation that we have at all times with a Liberal Government. The cost of living is rising faster than ever before. There is the intractable position of the Government in refusing to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on the one hand, while on the other we see Ministers [DOT] trying to encourage production in Canada, and export trade. Yet this Government persists in penalizing our manufacturers and penalizing the producers in Canada with this most atrocious tax. It seems to me that we are providing for low prices to primary producers, and this coupled with rising inflation and the cost of living has left our primary producers in Canada in a sorry state indeed.
Also, Mr. Speaker, they do not say anything in their Throne Speech as to what they are going to do about the economic situation in this country. They seem to be preoccupied with the cultural and welfare aspects and fail to realize that somebody has got to pay for it, somewhere, some time. Our friends in

the Social Credit Party have been true to form. The hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), who at the Christmas recess said he was going to topple this corrupt Government unless they did something about reorganizing their Cabinet, now comes before us and in his speech on six occasions commends this Government. They were the ones who were going to topple this Liberal machine. Then, of course, we have our friends in the New Democratic Party. I think they are going to go along with the Government, too.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I would like to quote very briefly from the Globe and Mail of this morning, "Looking Into Business", by Fraser Robertson. I think it is rather a good way to start on the criticism of this Throne Speech, this Univac attempt to gather votes. He starts out like this:
Any businessmen who had maintained until yesterday a conviction that business could be carried on as usual in Canada, or even businessmen who had lingering hopes that the entrepreneurial system based upon a market economy could survive in this country, surely must know better now that the Government has presented its legislative program to Parliament...
The wording is slightly different, but the measures are lifted almost intact from the manifesto of the New Democratic Party.
Then he goes on to make reference-and this is important-to the changes in rules and the procedural improvements which might be brought in, and I think all of us should keep in mind what he has to say in this regard:
Cynics might interpret that as a declaration that debate and criticism of Government measures is tolerable only if it does not impede passage of what the Government proposes.
The moral of this so far has largely been missed by business. It is that opposition to Government proposals, no matter how soundly based upon experience, largely is a waste of time.
Is that what we are coming to in our new rules changes? Is it going to be a waste of time to bother even opposing what a Government is going to insist upon? So we have this "Univac" Throne Speech, thrown out not to help the country but to try and improve the political image of the Government. We have a welfare approach to an attack upon poverty, but this welfare approach to poverty cannot be anything more than a stopgap. Production in Canada must pay for the welfare. There is precious little in this Speech for the people who are paying the bills.
I am going to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has been wrong in its approach to this problem, not only now but perhaps for a long time. For years we have been trying the wTelfare approach. This is
April 7, 1965	COMMONS
fine, and it meets immediate needs and ameliorates suffering. But it does not do anything about the basic problem. What about the one million jobs we are going to require? What about the jobs we need now? What about our productive capacity? What about medicare?-and I will have something more to say about that in a minute. What about ARDA? Whatever happened to the words the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) often used two or three years ago-"boldness", "imagination"? They are strangely lacking in this Speech.
I am convinced there is another answer to the problem. There is another position which the Government should take with regard to these problems. I do not believe that a "Big Daddy" type of Governmental system, in which the Government has to sit on the people like a setting hen on her chicks, will ever produce a great Government or make a great country out of us. We are so far behind in research and development in Canada that this minor item in the Speech from the Throne about a Scientific Council is like a drop in a pool of water. I do not mean we need any larger bureaucracy; Heaven's above, we have enough now. We have too many bureaucrats and we have precious little action. The Economic Council which this Government set up has cost a lot of money in order to provide some advice which the Government has largely ignored. We are losing right now, as mentioned by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), $2.8 billion a year in lost production.
What do we need in Canada? What should the Government's approach be? In my opinion we have to go back to what was said by the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) in his opening address. What is really needed is some kind of drastic action like that which motivated us during wartime. There is no drastic action in this Speech. I am suggesting that we should think about having a $2 billion research fund which could be spent over the next five years to help business to pay for this welfare program. We need research and development.
The hon. Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) talked about a medicare program.
I want to remind him that the major difficulty with the teaching profession is that they are all like square pegs in round holes. The difficulty with our educational system is that merit pays and individual initiative is forgotten. If we are going to have quality medical care let us not forget about individual initiative, because as both you and I
DEBATES	87
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner know, Mr. Speaker, so well, we will not have quality medical care without it.
What do we need before we achieve all this? We need a tremendous amount of regulation in Canada. We need a tremendous amount of money put into educational facilities to make available the medical personnel and technicians who are going to give this kind of care to all Canadians. Apparently the Government have no recognition of some of the problems which have to be looked into before we can achieve our objectives.
We in this Party have always stood for a national medicare plan based on freedom -freedom of the people who are providing the service and freedom of the patient to go to whom he pleases to get the service. We need tremendous amounts of funds to be made available to our universities and private enterprise for research into medical fields. This will do two things right away. It will provide the jobs which we need now and it will keep more of our best brains at home in Canada where they can do this type of research.
We also need research into our national resources. We need research into the matter of production, into the matter of marketing, into the matter of land use. We have had a Committee study land use, yet we know very little about the productive capacity in Canada of any of our soils. People talk about a population explosion, yet we are ignorant of what this really means in Canada. So this Government comes along with another welfare approach, instead of putting some money into a program of development and research which could stir up the country and do something to provide the one million jobs we are going to require very shortly. This research would provide some jobs immediately and would set the pattern to give us the one million jobs we are going to need in the next few years.
Coupled with this research we need development. I know the Liberal Party has been a stagnant party and does not like development. Their Members voted against a railway in Northern Alberta. They do not seem to think that this type of development is worth while. This is where government should be involved in initiating development and research, in getting private companies to go to work-because they are the people the Government is asking to pay the bills. We cannot keep taking a welfare approach to the question of poverty, because in the long term this will solve nothing. You can pay pensions and you can provide medical services, but unless you are going to provide

Very briefly, Sir, we need development along other lines in this country, and this Speech from the Throne is totally lacking in any of these directions. We need development of our human resources. We need some studies made with regard to leisure time and other social problems. We need development of our transportation system and research into transportation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has gone part way in this connection with his announcement the other day about airports. But we need more than that in Canada. We need landing rights for Canadian Pacific Air Lines in other cities in Canada, particularly Calgary and Edmonton. If we are to continue to be able to afford some of these welfare measures we need further development of our trade and marketing apparatus. We will have to get up off our fannies again and produce and package, market and sell. I do not see anything in this Speech from the Throne which will help us to do this.

The Speech from the Throne deals with international affairs. The best way that Canada can contribute to international affairs, in my opinion, is by setting an example here at home. Before we go rushing off into spheres into which we should not be, we should clean up our own backyard.
We need development in immigration. We need people in this country if we are going to develop our resources and have an adequate standard of living for all. We cannot do that through welfare projects. We cannot do that by adopting the superficial Univac political approach which this government has taken.
There is no doubt in my mind that we will support the subamendment because we have lost all confidence in this Government. They have bungled, they have led us up the garden path and they are completely inept as far as developing the country is concerned. We have no room in Canada for the Socialism of the Liberal Party; because with that Socialism we will have stagnation, and instead of raising the standard of living of the people of this country it will go down, because we will not be able to afford all these delightful welfare services which this Government would like to promise.
We need responsibility in Government and we should like to think that this Government would provide some leadership, but I am afraid there is no leadership there. There has not been any leadership provided by this Government for the great majority of the people in Canada who are paying the bills. This Government has not even suggested that it is going to do something about these problems. If we are not going to have production, if we cannot have employment and if we cannot have development, then we are not going to go very far, and we would be far better to take the $2 million and set up a research program.
The Department of Industry is not doing anything at this time. It could take over this research program and put it into effect through private establishments and we would then have a real start toward the development of this country. We must have this research and we must have it immediately, not only in respect of medical sciences but in respect of agricultural development and many other things. Let us stop putting the cart before the horse and return to some basic reasoning in this country, because we cannot continue to adopt welfare projects as a solution to poverty. Such a course will stagnate this country and will in the long run increase poverty.
Mr. Speaker, as you can see, I have lost any feeling that there is any semblance whatsoever of responsibility on the part of this Government. We therefore have no alternative but to kick them out and get back on the right road for the development of Canada.
